However, regular users should be encouraged to obtain the certificate of competence in radiotelephony, e.g. the Short Range Certificate (SRC) and if any other channels are available on the set the SRC is required. Channel 80 is an international channel and it may only be used by or under the direct supervision of someone holding a relevant Maritime Radio Operator’s Certificate and Authority to Operate. The CSR Licence will state that Channel 80 is available, but it would be best for the radio not to be programmed to have channel 80 (or any other international channel) available if there is no intention to use it and the operator does not hold a short range certificate. The CSR Marina Licence is renewable annually and is also available as a temporary licence, valid for up to 28 days to cover sporting and other special events.  Applications should be made to the Ofcom Licensing Centre.  As at May 2007, the fee is £75.00 for annual, and £20.00 for Temporary CSR Marina licences. Application forms are available at: http://www.ofcom.org.uk/radiocomms/ifi/licensing/classes/maritime /applications/of18.pdf

Where the radio on board has access to channel 80 (157.025/161.625 MHz) and/or other international channels, a separate licence must be held; two types of licence are available:-

section_titles: Ship Portable Radio Licence
text: The Ship Portable Radio licence allows a named licensee to have one VHF portable maritime radio for use on different vessels, using a “T number” call sign.  (The radio must have an integral antenna and power supply).  Other radio equipment such as one EPIRB/PLB can also be included; further details are available at: http://www.ofcom.org.uk/radiocomms/ifi/licensing/classes/maritime /information/of168a.pdf The Ship Portable Radio Licence is intended for use in UK territorial waters only. Obtaining a Ship radio or Ship Portable Radio licence – online Since December 2006, using the Ofcom website, boat owners have been able to apply online free of charge for a new licence or to amend the details of an existing one.  Paper based applications are subject to a one off fee of £20. Although there is no end date on the licence, licensees must validate their licence at least once every ten years.  There is no charge for validating your licence, and it can be done either online or by using a paper based application form. There is no charge for amending (or validating licences), whether done on-line or by post. If a licensee sells their vessel it is important for them to surrender their licence.  This can be done online or by using a paper based form. Should they purchase a vessel they should apply for a new licence indicating the details of the vessel’s call sign and Maritime Mobile Service Identity where applicable, as these must remain with the vessel. It is still a legal requirement for vessel owners that have radio equipment with access to international channels on board their vessel, to have an up-to-date radio licence.  They must keep these on board where practicable and in any case must be kept on board www.rya.org.uk

section_titles: Licences – Radio Equipment/Operator Certification:
text: Equipment whether ashore or aboard ship, must meet certain minimum approval requirements (e.g. “Wheel marking”/CE marking and comply with the relevant UK Interface Requirement, or have previously been type approved).  VHF equipment in every vessel having access to international channels must be under the control of an operator holding as a minimum, the Short Range Certificate and an Authority to Operate.  The Authority to Operate may be issued at the same time as the certificate of competence. Licences are valid only if the licensee/vessel/base station details accord with the details of the Licence.  Any changes in licensing details must be notified to Ofcom for re-issue of the licence as necessary.  There is no charge for this whether done online or by post.

text: **For safe and efficient shipping traffic in the Scheldt area**
text_with_context:
Source: VHF-procedures-Scheldt-area-EN.md  ·  Chapter: VHF PROCEDURES

[For safe and efficient shipping traffic in the Scheldt are — reference]
**For safe and efficient shipping traffic in the Scheldt area**

section_titles: FOREWORD
text:
These VHF procedures are a guideline for traffic controllers and traffic participants in the Scheldt area. Their aim is to clarify the use of VHF for safe and smooth shipping traffic. By correctly applying the procedures, other traffic participants will follow the good example, which will benefit safety.

The working procedures are based on the *IMO Guidelines For Vessel Traffic Services* (IMO Resolution A.1158(32)) and on the *IALA Guideline 1132 VTS Voice Communications and Phraseology*. In addition, various extra VHF regulations apply to specific vessel types, such as large gas tankers or oversized seagoing vessels. These regulations are not included in the general shipping procedures but are published via Joint Notices at www.vts-scheldt.net.

1. Definitions
text:
**Duty to be reachable (Bereikbaarheidsplicht)**
Every vessel equipped with a VHF radio must always be reachable on the correct VHF channel, as stated in these procedures.

**Port information**
Information about bridges, berths and lock planning.

**Pilot advice under Pilotage from a Distance / Remote Pilotage (LOA)**
If a pilot cannot perform his or her duties on board the vessel being piloted, he or she may give advice remotely to a master and/or traffic participant. That advice may be given from another ship or from ashore (a traffic centre), under certain conditions.

**Overflow function**
The use of an additional VHF channel to relieve the regular traffic channel, for example to provide navigation assistance or to conduct other lengthy conversations.

**Radar channel**
This channel has an overflow function relative to the traffic channel. A radar channel is used to relieve the traffic channel, for example to provide navigation assistance or port information, or to conduct other conversations. Reachability on the traffic channel remains mandatory in the meantime.

**Traffic instruction (Verkeersaanwijzing)**
An order or prohibition imposed to bring about a specific result in traffic behaviour. The order or prohibition is imposed by an authorised person on one or more traffic participants.

**Traffic arrangement (Verkeersafspraak)**
An agreement made directly between traffic participants themselves, in order to prevent unclear situations and/or imminent danger. Traffic arrangements must be made directly between traffic participants and not via a traffic centre.

**Traffic centre**
The location from which a traffic controller carries out his or her duties. Within the GNB (Joint Nautical Management) there are five traffic centres.

**Traffic participant**
A participant who has actual control over the navigation of a vessel.

**General traffic information**
Information provided by a traffic controller relating to one or more traffic participants within the area of operation. The information may be intended to support the on-board navigational decision-making process, to monitor and plan vessels, or to respond to the development of unsafe situations.

**Traffic controller**
A certified person who, from a traffic centre, ensures the safe and smooth handling of shipping traffic.

**Mandatory reports**
Reports that traffic participants must make at prescribed points or times in order to keep shipping traffic safe and flowing smoothly.

section_titles: 2. Purpose of a Vessel Traffic Service
text:
A Vessel Traffic Service is a service implemented by the authorities that provides the means to communicate with shipping traffic and to respond to situations developing within the VTS area. The service increases the safety and efficiency of shipping and contributes to "Safety of Life at Sea" and to environmental protection.

A VTS is responsible for:

- **Providing timely and relevant information** about factors that may influence navigation and that support the on-board decision-making process.
  This includes, among other things, information on the position, identity and destination of other ships, and hydrological and meteorological information.

- **Monitoring and planning vessels** so as to contribute to the safe and smooth handling of shipping traffic.
  This involves providing essential, up-to-date and timely information to support the on-board navigational decision-making process. This support consists of providing timely information, advice and instructions. The information may relate to anything in the chain of operations, such as lock planning, tidal windows, the availability of pilotage services, and so on.

- **Providing timely and relevant information** to respond to the development of unsafe situations.
  Essential, up-to-date and timely information is provided to support the on-board navigational decision-making process. This support consists of providing timely information, advice and traffic instructions.

To achieve this, a VTS can provide information, warnings or traffic instructions where necessary.

---

section_titles: 3. User philosophy
text:
If users of VHF channels do not observe communication discipline, cross-talk occurs. This cross-talk, also known as interference, disrupts normal message traffic and creates questions that do not benefit safety. To prevent interference on the VHF channels, VHF users must observe the following rules:

- All conversations over VHF must be short, businesslike and clear, and take place on the correct channel (communication discipline).
- All VHF installations must transmit at a power of no more than 1 watt.
- Within VTS-SG, a reporting obligation and listening-watch obligation applies to all commercial shipping.
- For recreational craft with a VHF installation on board, a duty to be reachable applies, but not a reporting obligation (see the folder *VHF Sectors in the Scheldt Area*).
- Monitoring the traffic channel is mandatory at all times. In case of congestion or other circumstances, a radar channel can serve as an overflow.
- If a traffic controller foresees bottlenecks or dangerous situations, he or she actively intervenes to prevent problems. The traffic controller uses his or her authority to give a warning, information, advice or a traffic instruction.
- Without prejudice to the powers of the Flemish and Dutch authorities, and in the context of the safe and smooth handling of shipping traffic, ultimate responsibility for navigation always rests with the master/traffic participant.
- Traffic arrangements between ships, such as passing or overtaking not in accordance with the applicable navigation rules, are made directly between the ships themselves. When crossing, reference is usually made to the colour of the sidelights, for example: "We are passing green to green." When overtaking, reference is usually made to the side, for example: "I am passing on the port/starboard side." This is the traffic-regulating character of such arrangements.
- All traffic participants and traffic controllers must comply with these prescribed VHF procedures.

section_titles: 3.1 Communication discipline for VTS Scheldt Area participants
3.1 Communication discipline for VTS Scheldt Area participants
3.1 Communication discipline for VTS Scheldt Area participants
text:
- **Maintain communication discipline**, even if other participants do not. - **Use the ship's name and the traffic centre's own name** in a call, not abbreviations or private names. - Traffic participants with a reporting obligation **report in on the relevant channel**. Reporting off again is not necessary, unless a mandatory report applies.

[SECTION BREAK]

- Traffic controllers ensure that **traffic participants make traffic arrangements among themselves** via the traffic channels. They may also mediate in this. - **Do not hold discussions** on traffic channels. - Use only the **approved working languages: Dutch or English**. In English, preferably use the Standard Marine Communication Phrases (SMCP). In an emergency, deviation from this is permitted.

[SECTION BREAK]

- Use **message markers** (in both Dutch and English) to make clear the type of message. In the management area of the GNA (Joint Nautical Authority), the Permanent Committee on Supervision of Scheldt Shipping has determined that the national language is also the working language in VHF communication. That is Dutch, with English as a fallback option (in accordance with SMCP). ---

section_titles: 4.1 Language proficiency check
text:
If there is doubt as to whether a waterway user is proficient in one of the mandatory working languages, the traffic controller will carry out a language proficiency check upon entry into the VTS-SG.

In the context of the chain of operations, the authorities of the ports adjoining the VTS-SG have issued similar instructions to their operational staff.

If the waterway user does not respond sufficiently clearly to a language proficiency check, the ship will not be admitted to the management area.

section_titles: 5. Indicators
text:
To promote communication discipline and to prevent overloading of the VHF channels in the VTS blocks, traffic controllers and all waterway users use the internationally established "message markers" to keep communication short, businesslike and clear.

These are the following eight indicators:

**MESSAGE MARKERS**

| Marker | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Information | Message contains observed facts |
| Question | Message has a questioning nature |
| Answer | Message is an answer to an earlier question |
| Intention | Message concerns intended navigational measures |
| Warning | Message is a warning of a potential danger |
| Request | Message asks the addressee(s) to take action |
| Advice | Sender wants to influence the addressee by means of a recommendation |
| Instruction | Sender wants to influence the addressee by means of a traffic instruction |

---

section_titles: 6. Navigation assistance
text:
The waterway user indicates when navigation assistance should be started and stopped by reporting in and out on the radar channel. The term **"navigation assistance"** is always used for this.¹

A traffic controller may also initiate the use of (elements of) navigation assistance on their own initiative in the event of deviant sailing behaviour.

- The traffic controller will confirm that the ship wants navigation assistance.
- In addition, the traffic controller will ask seagoing vessels in particular whether "buoy transits" (doorwisselen van boeien) are also desired.
  - Answer no: the traffic controller does not include the reporting of buoy transits as standard in the report.
  - Answer yes: the traffic controller includes the report of buoy transits (in a bend or during major course changes) as standard in the report.
- The waterway user then receives an initial message containing the following elements:
  - Understood/Acknowledged.
  - The own position of the ship that reported in for navigation assistance, according to the along/across method or the Bearing and Distance method (B/D method).
  - A relevant traffic picture of the ships in the vicinity.
- The traffic controller will also provide updates with the following content:
  - Own position of the ship according to the along/across or B/D method.
  - The aim is to provide this at least at every buoy or every second buoy, according to the traffic controller's assessment.
  - Update of the relevant² traffic picture, whereby work must also be done across block boundaries. Extra attention is given in this traffic picture to relevant overtaking manoeuvres and crossing traffic.
  - Any relevant passing distances, where applicable.
- Traffic arrangements must always be made on the traffic channel.

¹ No response is given to a request for assistance if reporting in is done using the terms "standing by" or "monitoring" on the radar channel.
² The information relevant to the traffic participant under navigation assistance (traffic, particulars, etc.) needed to form an up-to-date traffic picture in order to navigate smoothly, safely and efficiently.

section_titles: Explanation
text: - Traffic participants must indicate in good time if they wish to deviate from a route. - During navigation assistance, the traffic controller gives an overview of the current traffic picture, possibly supplemented with calculated, expected situations, such as encounters and passages in (passing) distance and time. - To convey the position of a moving ship, the position of the bow of the vessel relative to a point ahead in the fairway, or in bearing and distance, is used. For a stationary ship, this is the middle of the track or a radar echo. - The **passing distance** is the distance that will exist during passing between the adjacent sides of two ships, or between a ship and an obstacle. The passing distance is only reliable provided the ground track remains constant. - The **ground track** of a ship is its direction of movement relative to true north over the ground. - The **distance between two vessels** is the measured shortest distance. For head-on traffic this is the bow-to-bow distance; for overtaking traffic this is the bow-to-stern distance. - The **abeam distance** to a buoy, beacon or obstacle is the distance between the bow of a moving ship and an object, measured perpendicular to the direction of the fairway. - The **distance to a navigation mark** is the shortest distance to that navigation mark. - The terms **"opvarend" (upbound)** and **"afvarend" (downbound)** are used east of the Schone Waardin. In English these are "ingoing" and "outgoing". - In the approach areas and the roadstead area, the terms **"inkomend" (inbound)** and **"uitgaand" (outbound)** are used, in English "inbound" and "outbound". - To indicate a position before or beyond a certain point, we use **"bovenwaarts" (upstream)** or **"benedenwaarts" (downstream)**. In English these are "above" and "below". - If the traffic controller must give information about a part of the area not covered by radar and for which no visual information is available, he or she will make this known to the traffic participant requesting the information.

section_titles: Explanation
text: - Position information is always given relative to known reference points. These points are visible, known and can be found on the nautical chart. - A **bearing** between two known points is the horizontal angle relative to true north and the point being observed. The figures are spoken one by one. - **Distances** are given to a tenth of a kilometre or a tenth of a nautical mile (also called a "cable"). Where confusion is possible, e.g. between the English numbers fifty and fifteen, the digits are spoken separately. - Names of buoys and markers must not be translated. They are pronounced as they appear on the nautical chart. For example, W6 is pronounced "Whiskey 6". - "Buoy transit" (doorwisselen van boeien) refers to two consecutive buoys marking a bend in a channel coming into line relative to the bow of the ship. - Position reports can be given in two ways: using the along/across method, or via bearing and distance. The traffic controller may supplement this with ground track and ground speed. The intervals between reports depend on the traffic picture, the speeds of vessels, meteorological conditions, nautically critical points, and so on. - An **along/across position report** comprises, on the one hand, the point to which the ship has progressed along the length of the fairway, and on the other hand, the distance of the ship in the transverse direction, measured to the locally customary reference line — for example the buoy line, the light line, the shore, etc. The transverse distance may also be expressed as 1/3 red, 1/3 green, or mid-channel. If the distance is less than 1/3 of the fairway width, the distance is expressed in metres to the buoy line. Measurements are always given relative to the starboard side (SB) of the vessel. If this is not possible because there is no reference, the traffic controller will explicitly state this. - A **position report via bearing and distance** looks at the position of the forward part of the assisted ship in relation to a known point. Here too, the traffic controller may add ground track and ground speed. If the ship is sailing parallel to the reference line, moving away from it, or approaching it, this will be stated.

text:
- If the traffic controller gives position reports (on request) while a ship is coming to anchor, he or she agrees which point the reports will be relative to. Either the planned anchor position is indicated — this may be an anchorage as shown on the chart, or a position chosen by the master or pilot. From the bow, the traffic controller gives information by bearing and distance (B/D) to the anchor position, including speed over ground. As a standard for reporting frequency, the following applies:
  - Distance more than 1500 m: B/D every 500 m
  - Distance 1500 to 500 m: B/D every 200 m
  - Distance 500 to 200 m: B/D every 100 m
  - From 200 m: B/D every 50 m.

For anchor watch purposes, the master or pilot must state the number of nautical miles and/or cables relative to a fixed point, and the number of shackles on deck.

section_titles: 10.1 Principles
10.2 Area description, VHF channels and times
text:
The Scheldt Shipping Report (SSB) aims to provide information of a general nature to waterway users. The content of the SSB includes:

- Water levels and expected deviations at various measuring points in the area
- Expected cross-current reports off buoy 53
- Wind direction and strength at the traffic centre, storm warnings, local wind forecasts
- Visibility reports (where applicable)
- Shipping traffic, particulars and important works
- Significant deviations in fairway marking
- Depending on the traffic centre: pilotage information such as the side of the pilot ladder, storm pilotage, significant wave height at Kwintebank (GHs KWI) from 2.0 metres, and so on
- For Zeebrugge Traffic Centre only: traffic pictures within the area of operation concerning ships with a draught of ≥140 dm, or ships which, due to their tidal window (GNA), cannot deviate

[SECTION BREAK]

Four area-specific Scheldt Shipping Reports are broadcast. These are broadcast at different times so that they do not overlap.

Page 5 of 22 Introduction My first introduction to a VHF radio was while enjoying a weeklong sailing vacation around the Greek Ionian Islands. My husband, Simon, and I joined forces with another couple and hired a 33’ sailboat. The four of us became part of a sailing flotilla. Every morning, we would be briefed on our destination for the day. The vacation coordinators would ensure we left our mooring and help us dock up later in the afternoon. We had to use the VHF radio to communicate with the coordinators or ‘Lead Boat Crew,’ who kept close by. Thankfully, my husband and one of our friends handled all the communications, as my girlfriend and I were too scared to use the radio. I’m unsure what caused my fear of the radio – perhaps I didn’t want to make a mistake? Our initial sailing vacation ended up being a huge success. My husband and I were hooked for life. We enjoyed ten more years of sailing excursions and eventually purchased our first boat – a Moody 35’ sailboat. In the UK, where we kept our Moody, the maritime law requires that at least one person per boat possesses a Marine Radio Short Range Certificate (SRC). The SRC, which must be completed at a recognized training center, instructs users in radio etiquette and procedures, digital selected calling (DSC), and emergency procedures. Simon took the full-day course, passed the exam, and was granted a license. Fortunately for me, I once again dodged responsibility for the VHF radio. Side note: I have good news for you if you're in the US. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 permits recreational boaters to have and use a VHF marine radio, EPIRB, and marine radar without having an FCC ship station license. So, if you’re in the US, you don’t need a license; however, that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t learn how to use the VHF. VHF knowledge could mean the difference between life and death. Keep reading! Eventually, we traded our 35’ Moody for a 56’ Oyster sailboat, sold all our possessions, and decided to sail worldwide. At that point, I thought the time had come to face my fear of the VHF finally. But did I need to really take a course on the radio?

section_titles: Is a VHF radio course essential to take?
text: After sailing around the Solent, a massively busy waterway off England’s south coast, and listening to the VHF radio for a couple of years, I initially pooh-poohed the idea of getting my VHF License. Simon took the VHF radio course and obtained a license when we first purchased our boat, so as long as one person had a license, I felt OK to let him hold all the knowledge. And frankly, I always thought, ‘How hard can it be?’ I could quickly call up the marina and ask for a berth if I had to, so anything else would be similar. Yes? And if the worst-case scenario happened, and I had to make a MAYDAY call, I would push the scary red button on the radio and then follow the template taped to the underside of our navigation table left by the previous owner. What if… However, deciding to sell up and sail worldwide made me think twice about my VHF radio knowledge. If I did have to do a MAYDAY, would I do it correctly, considering the panic situation I’d most likely be in? Would I know how to figure out where I am? What if Simon wasn’t around and I received a DSC (Digital Selective Calling) alert – would I know how to respond? What is a DSC alert anyway? And what if our young daughter accidentally triggered the red button on the radio that is labeled ‘Distress’? Visit SailingBritican.com to become a confident sailing cruiser! Page 7 of 22

section_titles: The most important thing about sailing is safety
text: The most important thing about sailing is safety. If our boat is going to go down, my husband, crew, and I need to know exactly what to do. Furthermore, if someone else is in our vicinity and we can help to save lives, again, we need to know what to do. Hubby booked me on the VHF radio course. The pain of not knowing or having confidence in using the VHF radio became uncomfortable. Simon booked me on a VHF radio course in Southampton, England. Steve Gravells from Technical Recreational Coaching led a class of nine of us. Steve sent us the Royal Yachting Association (RYA) VHF radio course booklet a couple of weeks before the course, so we didn’t have to spend time learning the information from the book. If it weren’t for the homework that Steve requested before our class – a page of questions to be filled out – I would have failed to read the book. Again – I thought, ‘How hard can this be?’ Knowing I had homework to do, I read the book and did the homework. The RYA VHF radio booklet was beneficial. Aside from the first couple of pages filled with acronyms (R&TTE, DSC, SRC, CEPT) that I knew I would never remember, the RYA book was straightforward and easy to read. It took 30 minutes to get through, and I was full of information when I finished. Poor Simon had to listen to me say, “Did you know the word MAYDAY comes from the French word, M’aidez, and it means ‘help me’? And did you know that you need to send out a DSC (Digital Selective Calling) Alert before making a Pan-Pan voice broadcast?”

section_titles: Arriving at the Southampton Dry Stack after eating…
text: Arriving at the Southampton Dry Stack after eating a bacon roll, I was eager to put the day behind me. I’ve never been a fan of courses. I get bored quickly, and I wouldn’t say I like a numb bum – the sensation you get when sitting too long. Well, I was pleasantly surprised with the flow of the course. Never during the day did I wish that time would pass quickly. There was a mix of learning, watching, using the radio, coffee breaks, and general socializing. Everything taught was practical – it wasn’t theory or something that would go in one ear and out the other. And it was so powerful to see the difference between learning how to use the radio and then using it. Most of us seemed like we had it mastered, but when we went to (pretend) call another boat, the Coastguard, or make a MAYDAY, we found it more complicated than we thought. Ensuring to say who you are and whom you’re calling and finishing the message with the correct ‘over’ or ‘out’ wasn’t as easy as it looked! And talking slowly enough for others to write your MAYDAY was challenging. Not one person in the class spoke slowly enough for the other members to correctly note all the MAYDAY information. Thankfully, by the end of the day, the whole class sounded much better than when we started. That’s because Steve would have us go through the call if we didn’t get it right. To say that just my confidence increased would be an understatement. My faith, knowledge, and the importance of the subject matter increased. Learning how to use the VHF radio is not about making sure you can call a marina to request a berth – it’s a device to potentially save your life and the lives of those in your area. Until I took the course, I didn’t realize that the alarm that periodically went off on my boat was an urgent message alert. I didn’t know I was supposed to get a pen and paper Visit SailingBritican.com to become a confident sailing cruiser! Page 9 of 22

section_titles: So, is a VHF radio course necessary to take?
text: My answer is a definite ‘Yes.’ Unfortunately, it’s one of those situations where you don’t know what you don’t know. By taking the course, you’ll increase your confidence in using a VHF radio, understand how to maneuver your way around the menu system, and, most importantly, understand what to do when an emergency strikes. Overall, the VHF radio course is invaluable, and everyone in the boating community should take the course. Whether you take a VHF course or not, it is very easy to forget how to instigate a DSC distress or urgency message and follow up with the correct broadcast message. Furthermore, remaining calm in a potentially life-threatening situation or emergency can be challenging. By having quick, easy-to-understand, accessible instructions and broadcast templates, you make it easier for yourself to broadcast correctly and have a system that allows others who might not know how to use the VHF but are forced to do so. Within this guide, you’ll discover an explanation and an example of the various VHF calls, followed up with checklist templates ready for use. Furthermore, I’ve added various information, tips, and personal experiences to help make using the VHF radio easier. Taking a class is great, but if that’s not going to happen, this guide will provide you with everything you need to know to be a confident sailing cruiser. chapter_title: What is a VHF Radio, and why is it Important?
section_titles: What is a VHF radio?
text: A VHF radio is a two-way radio system that operates in the VHF frequency range, typically between 156.0 and 174.0 MHz. It is commonly used in the maritime industry and among sailors for emergency and routine communication. VHF radios are compact, easy to use, and designed to transmit and receive voice messages over relatively short to medium distances, making them ideal for maritime communication.

section_titles: Emergency Communication: VHF radios are a primary tool for emergency
text: communication on the water. Channel 16, often called the "distress channel," is dedicated to emergency calls. Sailors can use VHF radios to transmit distress signals (MAYDAY calls) when facing life-threatening situations, such as sinking, medical emergencies, or man-overboard incidents. Reliable Coverage: VHF radio signals have excellent coverage in coastal and open water areas, providing sailors with reliable communication even when far from shore. This makes VHF radios especially valuable for offshore sailing and long-distance cruising.

Coordinated Communication: VHF radios are often used to coordinate activities among a fleet of boats, such as buddy boats on group cruises. They enable sailors to stay in touch, share information, and assist if needed. During long passages with buddy boats, we’ll pick an unused channel and communicate about fish we’ve caught, thoughts on squall sightings, or do periodic check-ins.

Its importance cannot be overstated, as it enhances safety, facilitates coordination, and provides access to critical information while out on the water.

section_titles: A VHF marine radio consists of several components…
1. Main unit
text:
A VHF marine radio consists of several components that work together to provide communication capabilities for sailors. Here's an overview of the various parts of a VHF radio.

[SECTION BREAK]

A VHF radio's central unit houses the radio system's core components. It typically includes: • Transceiver: This is the heart of the radio, responsible for transmitting and receiving signals. • Power Supply: The central unit connects to the boat's electrical system or battery. • Antenna Connector: This is where you connect the VHF antenna, allowing the radio to send and receive signals effectively. It’s important to keep this clean.

section_titles: 2. Microphone
text: The microphone is an essential handheld component that allows the user to speak into the radio and control various functions. Key elements of the microphone include: • Transmit Button: This button, often labeled "Push to Talk" (PTT), is pressed when you want to transmit your voice over the airwaves. • Channel Selection: Many microphones have buttons or knobs to adjust channels and settings. • Volume Control: You can adjust the audio volume using a dedicated knob or buttons on the microphone. • Emergency Button: Some microphones have a dedicated emergency button to quickly access distress calls. 3. Controls
text:
VHF radios have various controls, typically located on the main unit and sometimes on the microphone. These controls allow users to configure and operate the radio, including: • Power Button: To turn the radio on and off. • Channel Selector: Used to choose the desired channel for communication. • Squelch Control: Adjusts the squelch level to filter out background noise when there's no signal.

section_titles: are in ‘grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance.’
text: MAYDAYS or Distress Alerts should be made only when immediate assistance is required for the vessel you are on. Examples include fire, explosion, sinking, major head or spinal injury, or man overboard. If immediate assistance is needed for another vessel, do not use this procedure. Consider doing a MAYDAY Relay if another boat is in trouble and unable to use the radio. Or use a MAYDAY Relay if a vessel calls the Coastguard and the Coastguard does not respond (described later). An example of a MAYDAY is as follows: MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY. This is Britican, Britican, Britican. section_titles: The VHF Radio Etiquette
text:
The VHF Radio Etiquette
As you embark on your sailing adventure, one of the essential skills you’ll need to master is the proper use of VHF (Very High Frequency) radio. This communication tool is vital for ensuring the safety of your vessel and crew, as well as maintaining good relations with fellow sailors and the maritime community. In this article, we’ll cover the basics of VHF radio etiquette, including proper procedures, common phrases, and tips for clear and effective communication.

section_titles: VHF Radio Etiquette Do’s and Don’ts
text:
Why VHF Radio is Important
VHF radio is a crucial tool for sailors, as it allows for communication with other vessels, marinas, and emergency services. It is essential for coordinating with other boats, receiving weather updates, and calling for assistance in case of an emergency. Additionally, proper use of VHF radio can help prevent accidents and misunderstandings, ensuring a safe and enjoyable sailing experience for all.

section_titles: VHF Radio Channels and Their Uses
VHF Radio Channels and Their Uses
VHF Radio Channels and Their Uses
text:
VHF radios operate on a range of channels, each designated for specific purposes. Here are some of the most commonly used channels and their functions:

Channel 16: This is the international distress, safety, and calling channel. It is used for making initial contact with other vessels or shore stations and for emergency communications. Once contact is established, you should switch to a working channel to continue your conversation.

[SECTION BREAK]

Channel 13: This channel is used for bridge-to-bridge communication between vessels, primarily for navigational purposes. Channel 9: In some areas, this channel is designated as an alternate calling channel for non-commercial vessels. Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A: These are common working channels for recreational boaters.

[SECTION BREAK]

Once you have established contact on channel 16, you can switch to one of these channels for your conversation. It’s essential to familiarize yourself with the specific channel assignments in your sailing area, as they may vary by region. Consult your VHF radio’s manual or local maritime authorities for more information.

section_titles: Basic VHF Radio Procedures
text:
To ensure clear and effective communication, it’s essential to follow proper VHF radio procedures. Here are the basic steps for initiating and conducting a VHF radio conversation:

Listen before transmitting: Before you begin speaking, listen to the channel to ensure it is not currently in use.
Select the appropriate channel: Choose the correct channel for your intended communication, as outlined in the previous section.
Press the transmit button: Hold the microphone about 2 inches from your mouth, press the transmit button, and wait for a second before speaking to ensure your transmission is not cut off.
State your call sign or vessel name: Begin your transmission by stating your vessel’s name or call sign, followed by the name or call sign of the vessel or station you are trying to contact. Repeat this process three times for initial contact.
Switch to a working channel: Once contact is established, agree on a working channel and switch to that channel to continue your conversation.
End your transmission: When you have finished speaking, release the transmit button and wait for a response. To conclude your conversation, state your vessel’s name or call sign and the word “out.”

section_titles: Tips for Clear and Effective Communication
VHF Radio Etiquette Do’s and Don’ts
VHF Radio Etiquette Do’s and Don’ts
VHF Radio Etiquette Do’s and Don’ts
text:
To ensure your VHF radio transmissions are easily understood, follow these tips for clear and effective communication:

Speak slowly and clearly, enunciating each word.
Use plain language whenever possible, avoiding slang or jargon.
Repeat important information, such as numbers or coordinates, for clarity.
Spell out words using the phonetic alphabet (e.g., Alfa, Bravo, Charlie) if there is any potential for confusion.
Keep your transmissions brief and to the point, avoiding unnecessary chatter.

[SECTION BREAK]

To maintain good relations with fellow sailors and the maritime community, it’s essential to follow proper VHF radio etiquette. Here are some do’s and don’ts to keep in mind:

Do:

Monitor channel 16 when not actively using your VHF radio, in case of emergency calls or important announcements. Use the lowest power setting necessary to communicate effectively, to minimize interference with other vessels. Be patient and courteous when communicating with other vessels or shore stations, even if they are not following proper procedures.

[SECTION BREAK]

Don’t:

Use profanity or offensive language, as VHF radio transmissions can be heard by anyone monitoring the channel. Engage in unnecessary chatter or lengthy conversations, as this can tie up the channel and prevent others from using it. Transmit false distress or emergency calls, as this is illegal and can result in severe penalties.

[SECTION BREAK]

By following these guidelines and mastering the art of VHF radio etiquette, you’ll be well-equipped to communicate effectively and safely with fellow sailors and maritime authorities. This essential skill will not only enhance your sailing experience but also contribute to the safety and enjoyment of all those who share the open sea.

Engage in unnecessary chatter or lengthy conversations, as this can tie up the channel and prevent others from using it. Transmit false distress or emergency calls, as this is illegal and can result in severe penalties.

[VHF Radio Etiquette Do’s and Don’ts — reference]
By following these guidelines and mastering the art of VHF radio etiquette, you’ll be well-equipped to communicate effectively and safely with fellow sailors and maritime authorities. This essential skill will not only enhance your sailing experience but also contribute to the safety and enjoyment of all those who share the open sea.

chapter_title: Vhf Radio Hardware, Installation And Handheld Care
section_titles: Antenna Cable And Connectors
text: The VHF antenna cable is a low-loss coaxial cable, typically RG-8X for shorter runs or RG-213 or LMR-400 for longer masthead runs, terminated with a PL-259 connector at the radio end and a matching connector at the antenna base. It carries the transmitted RF energy from the radio to the antenna and the received signal back down; a damaged, corroded, or poorly seated connector increases signal loss and can drastically reduce both transmit range and receive sensitivity even if the radio itself is working perfectly. The connector should be kept dry, greased with dielectric grease where exposed to weather, and checked periodically for a tight, corrosion-free fit.

chapter_title: Vhf Radio Hardware, Installation And Handheld Care
section_titles: Shutting Down The Radio Correctly
text: Before switching off, set the radio to Channel 16 or the intended standby channel, leave the volume at a normal level, and leave the squelch at its working threshold so the set is ready to go on next power-up. Note the last known GPS position and the UTC time in the log before shutdown, since a fixed-mount set may lose its live position feed once powered down. Press and hold the power key until the display switches off cleanly, rather than simply cutting external power at a breaker, which can occasionally corrupt saved settings.

section_titles: Volume And Squelch On A Handheld Radio
text: Rotate the volume control, often combined with the power button, or use the volume up/down keys until traffic is clearly audible over background noise. Rotate the squelch control, or the equivalent menu entry, fully open first so background hiss is audible, then gradually close it until the hiss just disappears; setting the squelch too tight will cause weak but genuine signals to be missed entirely.

text: Switch the handheld off, close any port flaps over the charging or accessory sockets, and secure or retract the antenna. Stow it in a dedicated wall-mount holder, or in a padded, water-resistant case, in a dry, ventilated locker that is still close enough to be reached quickly in an emergency, rather than in the bottom of a random bag where it is protected but slow to find.

chapter_title: Vhf Radio Hardware, Installation And Handheld Care
section_titles: Cleaning Contacts And Seals On A Handheld Unit
text: Power the unit off and remove the battery pack before cleaning. Wipe the metal battery-pack contacts and the corresponding contacts inside the radio body with a soft, dry cloth, or a cotton bud very lightly moistened with isopropyl alcohol; never use an abrasive material, which can scratch the contact plating and cause poor conduction later. Inspect the rubber gasket or O-ring seals around the battery compartment and any port flaps for grit, cracking, or compression damage, and gently clean them with a dry, soft brush, since a compromised seal is the most common cause of water ingress in an otherwise waterproof handheld.

section_titles: Charging A Handheld Radio Safely
text: Use only the charger supplied by, or explicitly approved by, the radio's manufacturer, since a mismatched charger's voltage or current can damage the battery or, in rare cases, create a fire risk. Charge in a dry, ventilated location, and avoid leaving a fully charged battery on trickle charge indefinitely for extended periods if the manufacturer's manual recommends periodic full discharge cycles to preserve battery capacity.

chapter_title: Vhf Radio Hardware, Installation And Handheld Care
section_titles: Checking The VSWR (Voltage Standing Wave Ratio) Of An Installation
text: A high VSWR reading indicates a poor match between the radio, the cable, and the antenna, usually caused by a damaged cable, a corroded connector, or an incorrectly tuned or damaged antenna, and it both reduces transmitted range and can, at extreme levels, damage the radio's output transistor over time. A basic in-line VSWR meter, inserted between the radio and the antenna cable, should read low (typically below about 1.5:1) on a healthy installation; a high or rapidly rising reading is a sign to inspect the cable run and connectors before the set is used for anything safety-critical.

chapter_title: Vhf Radio Hardware, Installation And Handheld Care
section_titles: Choosing A Mounting Location For A Fixed-Mount Radio
Basic Power Supply Considerations
text:
A fixed-mount VHF set should be mounted where it is reachable from the helm without leaving the wheel, protected from direct spray and sun, and with enough clearance behind the panel for the power and antenna cables to be connected without being sharply bent. Keeping the set close to the main power source reduces voltage drop in the supply cable, which can otherwise cause the radio to reset or transmit at reduced power during heavy current draw.

[SECTION BREAK]

A fixed VHF radio should be wired with an appropriately rated fuse close to the power source, not just at the radio end, and with cable heavy enough to avoid significant voltage drop over the length of the run; undersized power cable is a common, easily overlooked cause of a radio that transmits weakly or resets under load even though the antenna and cable to the antenna are both healthy.

chapter_title: Spelling Practice For Vhf Radio Communication
section_titles: Spelling out a word correctly on VHF radio is a core operato
text: Spelling out a word correctly on VHF radio is a core operator skill, required whenever a vessel name, a person's surname, a place name, or a technical term could be misheard due to static, weak signal, or similarly-sounding letters. Before spelling, the operator says "I SPELL" so the listening station knows individual letters follow rather than a normal word, then gives each letter using its NATO phonetic code word, and finally says "I SPELL" again followed by "OVER" to indicate the spelling is complete and hand the transmission back. The listening station should then read the spelled word back to confirm it was understood correctly. The examples below cover a wide range of realistic situations an operator will encounter: vessel names, surnames, given names, place names, waypoint and buoy names, cargo and technical terms, company and callsign fragments, harbor and port names, weather and position terms, and radio equipment terms.

text:
Q: Regarding WARNING: How should I express my position using latitude and longitude And in the context of 36_VHF_Exchanges — What does a 'WARNING' indicate in VHF communication? Please explain what each source says and combine into one recommendation. A: According to IMO standard marine comms phrases.pdf (NAV 46/WP.3): Guidelines for expressing latitude, longitude, and bearings in maritime communication. The steps are: express latitude and longitude in degrees and minutes; then use well-defined charted objects for marks; then report bearings in 360 degrees notation from true north; then quote bearings FROM the mark when reporting position. Use the prowords WARNING. Latitude and longitude must be expressed in degrees and minutes. According to 36_VHF_Exchanges.pdf (CONTACT PROCEDURE): The excerpt provides examples of communication exchanges on VHF radio.

Use the prowords QUESTION, WARNING, ADVICE. The term 'QUESTION' indicates a request for intentions. Combined recommendation on WARNING: Latitude and longitude must be expressed in degrees and minutes. Bearings should be reported in 360 degrees notation from true north.

[SECTION BREAK]

The term 'QUESTION' indicates a request for intentions. The term 'WARNING' indicates a safety hazard.

text:
AIS is installed on the majority of commercial vessels. Combined recommendation on AIS: EPIRB should be stowed near a companionway, helm station, or abandon-ship point. the SART detection range depends heavily on antenna height above the water. text: Q: Regarding AIS: How should I identify my vessel during a radio transmission And in the context of mgn_324 — What should I do if my AIS is not transmitting correctly? Please explain what each source says and combine into one recommendation. A: According to 5CVHF.txt (5cvhf): The excerpt discusses the importance of VHF radio communication in maritime navigation and the guidelines for effective communication. The steps are: use clear pronunciation; then identify yourself with your call sign; then keep communications concise; then ensure accuracy in position and speed reports. Use 13, 16. Use the prowords MAYDAY, PAN-PAN, SÉCURITÉ, OVER. VHF Channel 13 is primarily used for vessel-to-vessel communication. According to mgn_324.pdf (Radio and Automatic Identification Systems (AIS) at): Mariners using AIS on commercial vessels need to ensure proper operation and data transmission. The steps are: initiate action to correct improper installation; then ensure correct information on vessel’s identity, position, and movements is transmitted; then turn on the AIS at least within 100 nautical miles of the UK coastline; then check AIS data by contacting other vessels or shore stations.

Q: Regarding SAY AGAIN: are the consequences of making a false MAYDAY call And in the context of SailingBlogVHF — How do I identify my boat when using VHF radio? Please explain what each source says and combine into one recommendation. A: According to CompleteGuideVHF.txt (13 Bridge-to-bridge Navigation, bridges, locks, commercial traffic): The excerpt addresses the consequences of false MAYDAY calls and provides guidance on practicing radio procedures. The steps are: never make a MAYDAY call as a joke or for practice; then use Channel 9 for radio checks or call a friend; then immediately transmit a cancellation if a distress call is accidentally made; then monitor Channel 16 and explain the mistake to the Coast Guard if they respond. Use 9, 16. Use the prowords MAYDAY, I SAY AGAIN, THIS IS. False MAYDAY calls can cost tens of thousands of dollars in response resources.

[SECTION BREAK]

According to SailingBlogVHF.txt (Sailing Basics: How To Use A Vhf Radio): The excerpt provides guidance on using VHF radio communication effectively. The steps are: identify yourself using 'THIS IS' followed by your boat's name; then use 'OVER' when finished speaking and expecting a reply; then use 'OUT' when finished speaking and no reply is necessary; then say the name of the vessel you are addressing three times. Use 16. Use the prowords THIS IS, OVER, ROGER, WILCO, OUT, SAY AGAIN, REPLY.

[SECTION BREAK]

Channel 16 is primarily for distress calls and direct communication. Combined recommendation on SAY AGAIN: False MAYDAY calls can cost tens of thousands of dollars in response resources.

Please explain what each source says and combine into one recommendation. A: According to DSC_Menu_And_EPIRB_SART_Operation.txt (Dsc Radio Menu Operation And Epirb/Sart Handling): The excerpt provides guidelines for the proper storage and maintenance of EPIRBs and SARTs on a vessel. The steps are: stow the EPIRB in its dedicated bracket; then arm the Hydrostatic Release Unit (HRU); then visually check the bracket and HRU for corrosion or expiry; then stow the SART or AIS-SART close to the liferaft or grab bag. According to Ship radio information ofcom.pdf (Ship Radio Information): The excerpt discusses the registration and proper use of EPIRBs and PLBs for maritime safety. The steps are: register your 406 MHz EPIRB/PLB with HM Coastguard; then store your EPIRB safely on the vessel. An EPIRB/PLB is a battery-operated radio transmitter used in SAR operations. Combined recommendation on EPIRB: EPIRB should be stowed near a companionway, helm station, or abandon-ship point.

[SECTION BREAK]

the SART detection range depends heavily on antenna height above the water. An EPIRB/PLB is a battery-operated radio transmitter used in SAR operations. The EPIRB/PLB must have a unique identification code programmed during manufacture.

section_titles: 1. SOLAS Chapter IV — Radiocommunications
text:
**Source:** International Maritime Organization (IMO), International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, Chapter IV
**Link:** https://www.imo.org/en/About/Conventions/Pages/International-Convention-for-the-Safety-of-Life-at-Sea-(SOLAS),-1974.aspx

SOLAS is the core international treaty governing ship safety, and Chapter IV of its Annex deals specifically with radiocommunications. Its purpose is to guarantee that ships covered by the Convention are equipped so they can reliably send and receive distress and safety information, coordinate with each other and with shore authorities in emergencies, and call on organized search-and-rescue services when needed. The chapter also ensures that radio installations across different vessels and shore stations are technically compatible with one another, that they remain functional even after a single equipment failure (i.e., there is built-in redundancy), and that they are properly maintained throughout a ship's operational life. Chapter IV applies to all passenger ships on international voyages and to cargo ships of 300 gross tonnage or more on international voyages.

section_titles: 1. SOLAS Chapter IV — Radiocommunications
1. SOLAS Chapter IV — Radiocommunications
text:
It underpins the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS), the internationally standardized system of satellite and terrestrial communication procedures used for maritime distress alerting.

[SECTION BREAK]

The chapter has been substantially revised over time to keep pace with changing technology. A major modernization came into force on 1 January 2024 (via IMO Resolution MSC.496(105)), which updated the GMDSS to reflect the shift away from older systems. Under the revised chapter, ships operating in certain sea areas (A3/A4) are no longer required to carry high-frequency narrow-band direct-printing telegraphy (HF NBDP) equipment for transmitting and receiving distress and safety messages, and NAVTEX/EGC/HF NBDP receivers are no longer automatically mandatory — although owners may retain such equipment voluntarily for receiving maritime safety information. The amendments also broadened recognition of satellite service providers beyond Inmarsat to include other "Recognized Mobile Satellite Service" providers, such as Iridium, where a flag state accepts them. In UK law, SOLAS Chapter IV's requirements are given direct legal effect through the Merchant Shipping (Radiocommunications) (Amendment) Regulations 2021 (see Section 2 below), and MCA Marine Guidance Note 641 (M) explains how UK-flagged ships and operators should apply it in practice. ---

section_titles: Source:** UK Statutory Instrument, in force from 24 December 2021
text:
**Link:** https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2021/1316/contents/made

This Statutory Instrument is how the UK brings SOLAS Chapter IV into domestic law. It has two main effects. First, it directly imposes the SOLAS Chapter IV radiocommunications requirements on UK ships (and non-UK ships in UK waters) undertaking international voyages. Second, it amends the earlier Merchant Shipping (Radio Installations) Regulations 1998 so that ships on non-international voyages continue to have appropriate radio requirements, while ships covered by the Convention now only need to comply with the 2021 Regulations rather than the 1998 ones.

Structurally, the Regulations are organized into four parts. Part 1 covers general matters: citation and commencement, definitions, which ships the rules apply to, and provisions allowing the Secretary of State to grant exemptions or approve equivalent arrangements where full compliance would be unreasonable or impractical for a particular vessel. Part 2 sets out the basic functional requirement that ships must be able to transmit and receive distress and safety communications. Part 3 deals with the technical detail: performance standards for equipment, requirements for radio installations, watchkeeping obligations, maintenance duties, qualifications for radio personnel, record-keeping, and equipment testing. Part 4 covers enforcement — offences, penalties, and a ship's potential detention if it fails to comply.

A distinctive and important feature of these Regulations is the "ambulatory reference" provision (regulation 7). This means that whenever SOLAS Chapter IV is amended internationally in future, those changes are automatically incorporated into UK law at the same time, without needing a fresh Statutory Instrument each time. This keeps UK requirements permanently aligned with the current international standard.

The Regulations apply, with limited exceptions, to United Kingdom ships wherever they are, and to non-UK ships (including those from countries that haven't ratified SOLAS) while they are in UK waters.

---

section_titles: Source:** Maritime and Coastguard Agency
text:
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mgn-641-amendment-1-m-guidance-on-radiocommunications-under-chapter-iv-of-solas

MGN 641 (M) is the MCA's practical guidance document explaining how shipowners, masters, shipbuilders, and seafarers should interpret and apply the Merchant Shipping (Radiocommunications) (Amendment) Regulations 2021 described above. Rather than creating new legal obligations itself, it is meant to be read alongside the 2021 Regulations to clarify what compliance looks like in practice — and in fact parts of the Note have been given the force of law by the Regulations.

The guidance is structured around eight key topic areas: an introduction to the legal framework; how "recognised satellite service providers" are determined; requirements for radio installation on board; the sources of electrical energy that must be available to power radio equipment (including backup power in case of failure); the performance standards equipment must meet; maintenance requirements to keep radio equipment serviceable; qualifications and duties required of radio personnel on board; and the record-keeping obligations for radio logs.

Because the Regulations incorporate future SOLAS amendments automatically via the ambulatory reference mechanism, the guidance note is periodically reissued or amended (there have been at least one or two amendments since first publication in December 2021) to reflect the latest position and remove ambiguity for those applying the rules day to day.

---

section_titles: 4. Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006
4. Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006
text:
**Source:** UK Public General Act, 2006 c. 36, Parliament of the United Kingdom
**Link:** https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/36/contents

The Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 is the principal UK statute governing the use of radio apparatus of all kinds — not just maritime — including marine VHF sets. It received Royal Assent on 8 November 2006 and largely consolidated earlier wireless telegraphy legislation (including the Wireless Telegraphy Acts of 1949 and 1967) into a single, modernized Act, while also repealing a range of older enactments.

[SECTION BREAK]

It applies across the whole of the United Kingdom. The Act gives Ofcom its general statutory functions over the radio spectrum, including licensing radio apparatus and enforcing compliance. Two aspects of the Act are directly relevant to the misuse of VHF radio referenced in the PLA bulletin. Section 48 makes it a criminal offence to use wireless telegraphy apparatus to intentionally intercept the contents of a message not intended for the interceptor, or to disclose the contents, sender, or addressee of such a message obtained that way — a provision aimed at protecting the privacy and integrity of radio communications, including on marine VHF channels. Section 116 defines "wireless telegraphy" broadly, in essence covering the transmission or reception of electromagnetic energy up to 3,000 gigahertz used for conveying messages, sounds, or images, or for operating equipment, or for determining position or detecting objects — a definition wide enough to capture VHF, radar, and AIS. More broadly, operating radio apparatus without the required licence, or in a way inconsistent with licence conditions, is an offence under the Act, and this is the legal basis referenced by the PLA bulletin when it warns that "unnecessary transmission" or "non-standard phrases" on VHF may constitute a breach of the Act. The Act has been amended numerous times since 2006 (for example by the Digital Economy Acts of 2010 and 2017, and the Investigatory Powers Act 2016) to keep pace with changing telecommunications technology and enforcement practice.

section_titles: Source:** UK Statutory Instrument, in force from 26 December 2017
text:
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/radio-equipment-regulations-2017

These Regulations set out the technical and safety requirements that radio equipment (including marine VHF sets) must meet before they can legally be placed on the UK market or put into service. They were originally made to implement the EU's Radio Equipment Directive (2014/53/EU) into UK law and have since been adapted for the UK's post-Brexit UKCA (UK Conformity Assessed) marking regime, distinct from the EU's CE marking.

The Regulations' "essential requirements" (broadly in regulation/Article 3) require that radio equipment be constructed so that it protects the health and safety of users and other people (including domestic animals) and property; that it achieves an adequate level of electromagnetic compatibility, meaning it neither causes excessive interference to other equipment nor is itself unduly affected by interference; and that it makes effective use of the radio spectrum so as to avoid causing harmful interference to other radio users — a point directly relevant to why "unnecessary transmission" and "non-standard phrases" on VHF are discouraged, since spectrum efficiency is a legal design and use consideration, not just an etiquette one.

The Regulations place obligations on the various "economic operators" in the supply chain — manufacturers, importers, and distributors — including duties to prepare technical documentation, ensure conformity assessment procedures are followed, cooperate with enforcement authorities, and withdraw non-conforming equipment from the market if concerns are identified. Ofcom has powers to evaluate and act against radio equipment that presents a risk. The Regulations exclude certain categories of equipment from their scope, including some radio amateur and marine equipment governed by separate regimes, and they allow for different requirements in Northern Ireland reflecting its distinct post-Brexit trading arrangements.

---

section_titles: 6. ITU Radio Regulations
text:
**Source:** International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a United Nations specialized agency
**Link:** https://www.itu.int/pub/R-REG-RR

The ITU Radio Regulations are a binding international treaty — technically an integral part of the ITU's Administrative Regulations, which complement the ITU's Constitution and Convention — governing how the global radio-frequency spectrum (from 9 kHz to 300 GHz) and satellite orbits are used and shared among all 193+ ITU member states. They are the foundational document underpinning virtually all national radio law, including the UK's Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006.

The Regulations are revised roughly every three to four years by the World Radiocommunication Conference (WRC) to keep pace with new technology and changing spectrum demand, with the most recent full edition dated 2024. They are published in four volumes: Volume 1 contains the Articles (definitions, technical terms, and substantive rules, organized into chapters and numbered provisions); Volume 2 contains the Appendices (including detailed technical annexes such as those governing distress and safety frequencies); Volume 3 contains Resolutions and Recommendations; and Volume 4 contains ITU-R technical Recommendations incorporated by reference.

Of particular relevance to VHF maritime use, the Regulations define and classify various maritime radio services — the "maritime mobile service" (communication between coast stations, ship stations, and onboard units), the "maritime mobile-satellite service," the "port operations service" (restricted to messages about the operational handling, movement, and safety of ships, explicitly excluding general public correspondence), and the "ship movement service" (similarly restricted to messages about ship movements). This is the direct legal source for the PLA bulletin's requirement that VHF transmissions be strictly relevant to safety of navigation and operational coordination — the ITU treaty itself defines these radio services narrowly and excludes casual or personal messages from them by treaty definition. The Regulations also govern priority of communications (distress and safety traffic takes precedence), secrecy of communications, and the allocation of frequency bands (via the Table of Frequency Allocations in Article 5), which nationally-administered plans such as the UK's must follow.

---

section_titles: Source:** International Maritime Organization, Resolution A.918(22), adopted November 2001
text:
**Link:** https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Safety/Pages/StandardMarineCommunicationPhrases.aspx

The SMCP is a standardized set of English-language phrases developed by the IMO to reduce the risk of misunderstanding in verbal maritime communication, given that English is the internationally recognized working language at sea but is not the first language of most seafarers. It replaced an earlier, narrower document called the Standard Marine Navigational Vocabulary (SMNV), which had been in use since 1977.

The SMCP is organized into two parts. Part A covers essential phrases for external communication (ship-to-shore, shore-to-ship, and ship-to-ship) as well as onboard communication, focusing on navigation and ship handling — this is the part formally required for certification purposes. Part B is a supplementary, non-mandatory set of additional phrases intended to support wider maritime English learning. The phrases cover both routine situations (such as berthing and pilotage) and standard responses for emergencies, and are deliberately built on a simplified subset of English grammar and vocabulary to minimize ambiguity.

Under the STCW Convention (the International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers), officers in charge of a navigational watch on ships of 500 gross tonnage or above are required to demonstrate the ability to understand and use the SMCP as part of their certification. While the SMCP is primarily aimed at bridge-to-bridge and bridge-to-shore navigational safety communication rather than being a VHF-specific procedural rulebook, it is the natural companion to the PLA bulletin's requirement for clear, concise, and standardized language on VHF, since ad hoc or idiosyncratic phrasing is precisely what the SMCP was designed to eliminate.

section_titles: Source:** Maritime and Coastguard Agency
text:
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mgn-324-mf-amendment-2-navigation-watchkeeping-safety-use-of-very-high-frequency-vhf-radio-and-automatic-identification-system-ais

MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

---

section_titles: 9. Ofcom Ship Radio Licence Guidance
text:
**Source:** Office of Communications (Ofcom)
**Link:** https://www.ofcom.org.uk/manage-your-licence/radiocommunication-licences/ships-radio

This is Ofcom's guidance on the licensing regime for radio equipment carried on ships, covering medium frequency (MF), VHF, high frequency (HF), and ultra-high frequency (UHF) radio equipment, as well as satellite communications, radar, Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacons (EPIRBs), and Search and Rescue Transponders (SARTs). The stated purposes of licensing are twofold: to prevent radio equipment from causing undue interference to other users of the spectrum, and to ensure equipment is operated only by competent, appropriately trained individuals.

Historically a UK "Ship Radio Licence" required annual renewal and a fee, but following a 2005 Ofcom consultation and policy change, ships' radio licences became "lifetime" licences from 1 October 2006 — free of charge, issued electronically, with no fixed expiry date, remaining valid as long as the registered details stay accurate (though licensees must periodically reconfirm their details). A licence is personal to the licensee and does not automatically transfer if a vessel is sold. Separately from the equipment licence, the individual operating the radio needs an operator's qualification — for VHF-only use this is the Short Range Certificate (SRC), obtained via a one-day training course covering radio procedure, etiquette, and use of Digital Selective Calling (DSC); a Long Range Certificate (LRC) is needed for other, longer-range communications equipment.

Operating marine radio equipment without both the required ship licence and a valid operator's certificate is a criminal offence. [9. Ofcom Ship Radio Licence Guidance — rule]
**Source:** Office of Communications (Ofcom)
**Link:** https://www.ofcom.org.uk/manage-your-licence/radiocommunication-licences/ships-radio

This is Ofcom's guidance on the licensing regime for radio equipment carried on ships, covering medium frequency (MF), VHF, high frequency (HF), and ultra-high frequency (UHF) radio equipment, as well as satellite communications, radar, Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacons (EPIRBs), and Search and Rescue Transponders (SARTs). The stated purposes of licensing are twofold: to prevent radio equipment from causing undue interference to other users of the spectrum, and to ensure equipment is operated only by competent, appropriately trained individuals.

Historically a UK "Ship Radio Licence" required annual renewal and a fee, but following a 2005 Ofcom consultation and policy change, ships' radio licences became "lifetime" licences from 1 October 2006 — free of charge, issued electronically, with no fixed expiry date, remaining valid as long as the registered details stay accurate (though licensees must periodically reconfirm their details). A licence is personal to the licensee and does not automatically transfer if a vessel is sold. Separately from the equipment licence, the individual operating the radio needs an operator's qualification — for VHF-only use this is the Short Range Certificate (SRC), obtained via a one-day training course covering radio procedure, etiquette, and use of Digital Selective Calling (DSC); a Long Range Certificate (LRC) is needed for other, longer-range communications equipment.

Operating marine radio equipment without both the required ship licence and a valid operator's certificate is a criminal offence. Ofcom's enforcement team can issue on-the-spot fines, and the maximum penalty on conviction is a £5,000 fine and/or up to six months' imprisonment, with the possibility of forfeiture of any radio apparatus used unlawfully. This is the direct legal underpinning of the PLA bulletin's warning that improper VHF use may lead to penalties enforced by Ofcom.

section_titles: Basic Communication Structure
text:
Professional VHF communication follows structured patterns that ensure message clarity while reducing transmission time and preventing channel congestion during busy maritime operations.

Essential communication elements include:
► Station identification: Clear vessel name and call sign identification
► Message markers: Instruction, advice, warning, information, question, answer, request, intention
► Standard responses: Affirmative and negative acknowledgments with full repetition
► Position reporting: Precise location using degrees, minutes, and geographic references
► Time references: UTC notation with clear hour and minute designations

Example (Initial Contact):

Vessel A: "Port Control, Port Control, this is MV Ocean Star, 
call sign Hotel Alfa Bravo Charlie One, on Channel One-Two. 
How do you read me? Over."

Port Control: "MV Ocean Star, this is Port Control. 
Reading you loud and clear. Go ahead. Over."

section_titles: Spelling and Number Conventions
⌑ Letters: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel
text:
International phonetic alphabet usage ensures accurate information transmission when spelling becomes necessary during radio communications. Standardized number pronunciation prevents confusion that could result in navigation errors or operational mistakes.

Standard phonetic alphabet includes specific pronunciations:

[SECTION BREAK]

⌑ Numbers: Zero (ZEERO), One (WUN), Two (TOO), Three (TREE)
⌑ Special numbers: Four (FOWER), Five (FIFE), Eight (AIT), Nine (NINER)
⌑ Large numbers: Thousand (TOUSAND) with individual digit pronunciation

Position coordinates require careful pronunciation using individual digits for degrees and minutes, followed by cardinal directions. Bearing references use three-digit notation from true north unless specifically stated as relative bearings.

❔ Did you know? Modified number pronunciation reduces confusion between similar-sounding digits during radio transmission, especially in challenging atmospheric conditions.

section_titles: ► Standard Marine Communication Phrases are mandatory for of
text:
► Standard Marine Communication Phrases are mandatory for officers in charge of navigation watch on vessels over 500 gross tonnage
► Message markers must precede communications to clarify intent: instruction, advice, warning, information, question, answer, request, intention
► Phonetic alphabet uses specific pronunciations like ZEERO for zero, WUN for one, and FOWER for four to prevent transmission errors
► Position reporting requires degrees and minutes with cardinal directions, avoiding decimal degrees for radio communication
► Time references must use UTC notation clearly stating hours and minutes to prevent timezone confusion
► Emergency communication hierarchy progresses from MAYDAY (distress) through PAN-PAN (urgency) to SECURITE (safety)
► VTS communications require accurate vessel information including dimensions, cargo details, and operational restrictions
► Pilot communications address boarding arrangements, safety equipment, and weather conditions before transfer operations
► Weather reporting follows meteorological standards using cardinal points for direction and Beaufort scale for wind force
► Bridge team communication requires systematic information sharing with clear command acknowledgment procedures

section_titles: June 4, 2024
text:
What is the correct way of talking on a marine VHF radio? You must use the proper channel for the given situations, communications must follow protocol, and the right language and terminology must be used for every transmission.

A key aspect of being at sea is safety. A VHF marine radio is a means of communication for all situations, particularly emergencies.

And in urgent situations, the last thing you want is for your calls to be lost in translation.

Talking on a VHF marine radio requires you to use the correct channels relative to your needs and know how to communicate your location. Using appropriate vocabulary, knowledge of the NATO (phonetic) alphabet, and following step-by-step protocol for conveying messages is vital.

When using VHF radios for marine communication, finding a channel, tuning in, and starting a conversation is not straightforward.

Below, I will explain the correct procedure, the language and terminology used while talking on a marine VHF radio, the appropriate channels, and what is considered bad etiquette.

Contents (TLDR)

How Should You Talk On A Marine VHF Radio?
First of all, you should be aware of who can use a marine VHF, and then you can follow protocol for VHF radio comms at sea.

This is true for emergencies and other communication. The steps are listed below for non-emergency-related communications.

section_titles: 1️⃣ Identify Your Needs
text: Why are you trying to establish communication? Even for non-urgent matters, you must know the best and most concise way to verbalize your needs via marine VHF radio.
text_with_context:
Source: VHFProtocolsUS.txt  ·  Chapter: vhfprotocolsus

[1️⃣ Identify Your Needs — definition]
Why are you trying to establish communication? Even for non-urgent matters, you must know the best and most concise way to verbalize your needs via marine VHF radio.

section_titles: 2️⃣ Identify Your Point Of Contact
text:
Who are you trying to communicate with? This may be another vessel, the marina, or anyone else in the vicinity with a VHF radio.

You also cannot make a general call to anyone in particular and hope for a response. This is not only bad etiquette but also an incorrect procedure. A call must be made to a specific station or vessel.
